headline: Virginia senator seeks probe of Louise Lucas over federal marijuana charges
dek: Republican Sen. Bryce Reeves prefiled Senate Resolution 173, asking a committee to examine Sen. Louise Lucas's indictment and weigh expulsion.
key_points: Sen. Bryce Reeves prefiled Senate Resolution 173 on 30 October, sending the federal case against Sen. Louise Lucas to the Committee on Privileges and Elections for the 2027 session.

A federal indictment unsealed on 22 October charges Lucas with five counts, including racketeering, marijuana distribution and honest-services fraud conspiracies; none of the allegations has been proven.
Expelling a senator takes 27 of 40 votes, so at least eight Democrats would have to join all 19 Republicans.
Prosecutors allege Lucas held an undisclosed stake tied to a prospective adult-use licence, as Virginia prepares to open retail cannabis sales.
body: A Republican Virginia senator wants the state Senate to investigate one of its most powerful Democrats and consider expelling her over federal marijuana charges. Sen. Bryce Reeves of Spotsylvania prefiled Senate Resolution 173 on 30 October for the 2027 General Assembly session. It asks the Committee on Privileges and Elections to examine the allegations in a federal indictment against Sen. L. Louise Lucas of Portsmouth, the Senate's president pro tempore and chair of its Finance and Appropriations Committee.

Lucas has not been convicted of anything and has said federal authorities are trying to intimidate her. The resolution itself states that she is presumed innocent and that the committee should not treat the indictment or any statement quoted in it as proof. What it seeks is a parallel inquiry by the Senate into whether her conduct broke Virginia's conflict-of-interest and disclosure rules, with expulsion as one possible outcome.

According to the resolution, a federal grand jury returned the indictment on 14 October in the Eastern District of Virginia, and it was announced on 22 October. It names Lucas in five counts: racketeering conspiracy, conspiracy to distribute and possess with intent to distribute marijuana, conspiracy to commit money laundering, conspiracy to commit honest-services fraud, and maintaining drug-involved premises. Six other people, including relatives and business associates, were also charged, according to the Virginia Mercury.

Prosecutors allege Lucas helped run a marijuana distribution business connected to The Cannabis Outlet and The CBD Shoppe, laundered proceeds and used her office for personal gain. One allegation, as summarised by the Mercury, centres on a $750,000 payment Lucas allegedly made in 2022 for an ownership interest in a business tied to another person's expected adult-use licence, an interest prosecutors say she did not disclose. The investigation became public in May, when federal agents searched her legislative office and the businesses.

SR 173 directs the committee to obtain recordings, transcripts, financial and ownership records, statements of economic interests and legislative records. It singles out two statements attributed to Lucas in paragraphs 103 and 104 of the indictment: one in a March 2026 discussion about legalising past marijuana-related conduct, and one in an 11 March call in which she allegedly talked about disqualifying a prospective licence applicant until money owed to her was repaid. The committee is asked to test the authenticity and context of those statements rather than accept them.

If the committee finds discipline is warranted, a further resolution would be needed. Options under the Senate rules include reprimand, censure, expulsion or referral to the attorney general. Reeves told the Mercury the review might not lead to expulsion.
> The case puts Virginia's own cannabis licensing on trial in the court of public opinion just as the state prepares to hand out retail licences.

Under the Virginia Constitution, expelling a senator requires two-thirds of the elected membership: 27 of 40 senators. Democrats hold 21 seats. If all 19 Republicans voted to expel, at least eight Democrats would have to join them. Gov. Abigail Spanberger has defended Lucas's right to a defence and questioned the timing of an indictment unsealed less than two weeks before the midterm elections; federal authorities have said the investigation began before President Donald Trump returned to office.

The committee may not move quickly. Its chair told 13News Now on 30 October that he had not received any resolution from the clerk and that no meetings were scheduled before the session. The resolution is formally offered on 13 January 2027.
## Why it matters for Virginia's market

The allegations go to the heart of how Virginia will license its adult-use market. As we reported on 7 November, a report for the Virginia Cannabis Control Authority estimates residents spend about $1.05 billion a year on cannabis and recommends keeping the legal cap of 350 retail licences, issued in phases. Any suggestion that a senior lawmaker sought to influence who gets a licence will shadow that process and give ammunition to those who want tighter rules on who may hold a stake.

Virginia's medical market, by contrast, is already inside the federal system. Virginia was one of the seven states in the DEA's first wave of Schedule III registrations, MJBizDaily's count shows no Virginia dispensary applications still pending, and Jushi says all of its Virginia dispensaries were registered.

Watch the federal docket for arraignment and trial dates, and the Senate's opening on 13 January, when SR 173 is formally offered and referred. Watch also for any move by lawmakers to tighten disclosure rules for interests in cannabis licences before retail licensing opens.
